title: The Fall of the Vital Force

scenes.tts: For most of the history of science, the molecules of living things were thought to need living things to make them. Sugar, fat, urea: all of it was supposed to carry a vital force. The chemist Berzelius drew the line. Inorganic matter, the chemistry of rocks and salts, obeyed ordinary law. Organic matter, the chemistry of living bodies, did not.
scenes.visual: Two kingdoms split by a wall: inorganic (rocks, salts) vs organic (sugar, fat, urea) with a spark/vital force label.
scenes.narration: For most of the history of science, the molecules of living things were thought to need living things to make them. Sugar, fat, urea: all of it was supposed to carry a vital force. The chemist Berzelius drew the line. Inorganic matter, the chemistry of rocks and salts, obeyed ordinary law. Organic matter, the chemistry of living bodies, did not.

scenes.tts: In February 1828, Friedrich Wöhler warmed an inorganic salt, ammonium cyanate. What crystallized in his flask was urea, the molecule the body makes to dispose of nitrogen. There was no kidney in the room. Both compounds have the same formula: one carbon, four hydrogens, two nitrogens, one oxygen. Same atoms, connected differently. Heat rearranged the connections.
scenes.visual: Ammonium cyanate chip heated into urea chip; identical atom-count tally bars stay while the name and the kingdom change.
scenes.narration: In February 1828, Friedrich Wöhler warmed an inorganic salt, ammonium cyanate. What crystallized in his flask was urea, the molecule the body makes to dispose of nitrogen. There was no kidney in the room. Both compounds have the same formula: one carbon, four hydrogens, two nitrogens, one oxygen. Same atoms, connected differently. Heat rearranged the connections.

scenes.tts: Wöhler's flask did not kill vitalism that afternoon. His critics had an honest objection: ammonium cyanate could be traced back to organic sources. The vital force pulled back, but it had somewhere to stand. In 1845 Hermann Kolbe built acetic acid from carbon disulfide, made from charcoal and molten sulfur, with nothing alive in the chain. A decade later Marcellin Berthelot built fats from glycerol and fatty acids.
scenes.visual: Territory left for the vital force shrinks in steps: Wohler objection, Kolbe lifeless chain, Berthelot fats.

scenes.tts: One redoubt remained. Louis Pasteur had proved that fermentation depends on living yeast. From this he drew a stronger line than his data required: that fermentation was inseparable from the intact living cell. That conviction held for forty years. In 1877 Wilhelm Kühne proposed the word enzyme, from the Greek for in leaven, for the soluble agent inside yeast.
scenes.visual: Timeline strip; remaining territory is whole processes inside a cell; Pasteur fence around cell; Kuhne names the worker inside.

scenes.tts: In 1897 Eduard Büchner ground brewer's yeast with sand and pressed out a clear golden juice with no intact cells in it. He added sugar to preserve it. The sugar began to ferment, carbon dioxide rising through a flask of dead yeast. Vitalists said living scraps must have survived. Büchner ran two controls. Boiled juice did not ferment, so the agent was a destructible chemical. Filtered juice still did, so no cells were needed.
scenes.visual: Yeast cells to press to juice to flask with CO2 bubbles; boiled flask no bubbles; filtered flask still bubbles; territory goes to zero.

scenes.tts: Seventy years of syntheses made the vital force unnecessary, one molecule and one process at a time. What replaced it is the premise of this course: a living cell obeys the same chemistry as everything else, with no separate law of its own. The catalysts Kühne named and Büchner freed are ordinary proteins.
scenes.visual: Wall dissolves, one kingdom: cell inside chemistry; enzyme chips as ordinary proteins; Kolbe/Wohler/Buchner milestones resolved.
